fields.foundation: The Almoravid Empire began among Saharan Berber nomads who followed a reformist Islamic preacher. Within some seventy years they ruled a territory stretching roughly three thousand kilometres, from the Senegal River to the Ebro in northern Spain. The movement started around 1035–1040 CE, when Yahya ibn Ibrahim, a chieftain of the Godala (Gudala) tribe returning from pilgrimage to Mecca, met the Fez-born Maliki jurist Abu Imran al-Fasi in Kairouan and was eventually provided with a teacher, Abdallah ibn Yasin, to instruct his people in orthodox Maliki practice. The Godala rejected Ibn Yasin. He found a more receptive audience among the neighbouring Lamtuna and, according to tradition, established a ribat, a fortified religious community, that became the movement's religious and military centre. Its members called themselves al-Murabitun, "the people of the ribat", which Spanish rendered as Almorávides. The Almoravids captured Sijilmasa, the northern terminus of the trans-Saharan gold trade, in 1054–1055, and soon afterwards Awdaghust in the south. Along this route gold from the Bambuk and Bure fields of the upper Senegal and Niger went north to Mediterranean markets, and control of it paid for the movement's conquests for decades. Marrakesh, founded around 1070 (traditionally 1062), became the capital of the northern branch under Yusuf ibn Tashfin. In 1086 he crossed the Strait of Gibraltar at the invitation of the Andalusian taifa kings, the rulers of petty Muslim principalities who could not on their own resist the advance of Alfonso VI of Castile, conqueror of Toledo in 1085.
fields.socioeconomy: The Almoravid economy rested on three things: control of the trans-Saharan gold trade, the agricultural revenues of Morocco and western Algeria, and the urban economy of al-Andalus. The trans-Saharan trade brought enough West African gold to the Mediterranean to make the Almoravid gold dinar one of the most trusted currencies of the medieval Mediterranean. It was prized for its purity and so widely used that Christian Iberia imitated it as the morabetino, the origin of the Castilian maravedí. The gold gave the Almoravid treasury revenues that flowed regardless of harvests, and from them it could finance campaigns, build mosques, fortifications and public works, and maintain a professional fighting force. Morocco provided grain, livestock and pastoral products from the Atlantic plains. Andalusian irrigated agriculture, the huertas of Valencia, Murcia and Granada, drew on a hydraulic tradition that built on Roman foundations and techniques introduced from the Islamic East, and it produced surpluses that supported dense urban populations. The austere Saharan Berber warrior class that formed the military and ruling elite stood apart from the cosmopolitan Andalusian urban civilisation it had conquered. Under Ali ibn Yusuf (r. 1106–1143), Andalusian culture crossed the Strait into Marrakesh: Andalusian secretaries, artists and architects rebuilt the capital and brought urban institutions, architectural refinement and learning far removed from the desert tradition from which the dynasty had sprung. The court's adoption of this culture left the empire exposed to the same puritanical critique it had used against others.
fields.military: The early Almoravid armies drew their strength from the Lamtuna and allied Sanhaja Berbers of the western Sahara, veiled warriors hardened by the desert, whose endurance, discipline and cohesion the armies of Morocco and al-Andalus could not match. The Almoravids fought in disciplined infantry ranks armed with long spears and javelins, backed by cavalry, and they used massed war drums to coordinate manoeuvres and unnerve opponents. Their camels, whose smell unsettled horses, reportedly helped to disrupt enemy cavalry. At the Battle of Sagrajas (al-Zallaqa in Arabic) on 23 October 1086, Yusuf ibn Tashfin's army shattered Alfonso VI's forces near Badajoz. It was one of the most decisive victories in Iberian history and halted the Christian advance. The taifa kingdoms were then absorbed: Granada in 1090, Seville in 1091, Badajoz in 1094 and Zaragoza in 1110. Military pressure was joined to legal justification. Before deposing the taifa rulers, Yusuf obtained fatwas from Maliki jurists condemning them for impiety and illegal taxation, which framed conquest as religious correction. The fatal weakness was the small size of the Saharan elite: the empire was trying to garrison both Morocco and al-Andalus with a pool of desert warriors that could not be quickly replaced. As this elite aged, it was supplemented by Christian mercenaries under commanders such as the Catalan Reverter and by Andalusian levies, and the army lost the character and the edge it had begun with. By the 1130s the Almoravids were fighting losing wars at once against Christian armies in the north and the Almohad insurgency in the Atlas Mountains.
fields.governance: Almoravid government combined desert tribal authority with the urban administration inherited from the Andalusian taifa tradition. Yusuf ibn Tashfin took the title Amir al-Muslimin, Commander of the Muslims. He deliberately stopped short of the caliphal title and acknowledged the nominal supremacy of the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, while ruling his domains as an independent sovereign. The administrative machinery of the Andalusian cities was largely preserved after conquest: existing secretaries and jurists were retained under Almoravid governors, often members of the ruling family, so that the empire could function without the Lamtuna warriors needing administrative skills they did not possess. Maliki jurisprudence was the empire's law. Maliki scholars enjoyed enormous prestige and political influence at court, and they supplied the religious legitimacy that justified both the original conquests and continuing tax demands; under Ali ibn Yusuf their influence extended to the public burning of the works of al-Ghazali. Marrakesh was the capital, and under Ali ibn Yusuf it grew from a military encampment into a city with mosques, baths, mills, an underground water supply and caravanserais built to Andalusian standards. The two halves of the empire, Saharan Morocco and urban al-Andalus, had little in common culturally, economically or socially. The dynasty kept separate administrative traditions under a unified military hierarchy. This worked as long as that hierarchy remained capable and cohesive, but it proved fragile once Christian advance on one front and Almohad insurgency on the other undermined Almoravid military credibility.
fields.impact: The Almoravid intervention in Iberia preserved Muslim rule over much of southern Spain for a century and a half beyond what the fragmented taifa kingdoms could probably have achieved alone. Without the victory at Sagrajas in 1086, Alfonso VI's Castile might have overrun much of al-Andalus before the end of the eleventh century, altering the course of Iberian and European history. The empire's control of the trans-Saharan gold trade channelled West African wealth into the Mediterranean economy. The Almoravid dinar was a benchmark of monetary reliability in the western Mediterranean for decades, and its name survives in the Iberian maravedí. The dynasty brought together Saharan Berber, Moroccan and Andalusian traditions in architecture and art, and the Almohad and Marinid dynasties built on their work. The resulting Hispano-Moresque style is visible in monuments such as the Qubba Ba'adiyyin in Marrakesh, the Great Mosque of Tlemcen and the Qarawiyyin Mosque in Fez, which Ali ibn Yusuf enlarged. The absorption of the taifas also brought the jurists, physicians, geographers and poets of al-Andalus under a single government, creating conditions for exchange across the Strait. In West Africa, the southern branch under Abu Bakr ibn Umar helped spread Maliki Islam through the Sahel, contributing to the Islamisation of the western Sudan and shaping the religious character of the later Mali and Songhai empires.
fields.decline: The Almoravid Empire fell as quickly as it had risen: from the death of its greatest ruler, Yusuf ibn Tashfin, in 1106 to the fall of Marrakesh in 1147, just forty-one years elapsed. A small Saharan Berber military elite was trying to govern a large and highly cultured Andalusian and Maghrebi society. The Almoravids had conquered al-Andalus by arguing that the taifa kings were insufficiently Islamic; their successors the Almohads conquered the Almoravids with the same argument. The Almohad movement, launched by Ibn Tumart in the Atlas Mountains around 1121, denounced the Almoravids as anthropomorphist heretics who had succumbed to luxury and oppressed their subjects with unlawful taxation, much the same charges the Almoravids had levelled against the taifas. The Almoravids could not easily answer, because their own legitimacy rested on an identical claim to religious purity. Meanwhile the northern front deteriorated. Zaragoza, the chief city of the Ebro valley, fell to Alfonso I of Aragon in 1118, and after the Battle of Ourique in 1139 Afonso Henriques assumed the title of King of Portugal. Ali ibn Yusuf and his son Tashfin ibn Ali failed in campaign after campaign to destroy the Almohads. Tashfin's death near Oran in 1145 opened Morocco to the Almohads. In 1147 Abd al-Mu'min's forces stormed Marrakesh, killed the last Almoravid ruler, the young Ishaq ibn Ali, and demolished Almoravid monuments, including the palace on whose site the Koutoubia Mosque would rise.
fields.summary: The Almoravid Empire was a dynasty of desert puritans that saved Muslim al-Andalus from Christian conquest and then took up the very urban culture it had professed to disdain; the conquerors were changed by what they conquered.
fields.teaser: A Berber dynasty that arose from religious reformers in the Sahara, the Almoravids united the Maghreb and al-Andalus and checked the Christian advance at the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086.
fields.t0: Saharan Berber reformists who built an empire from the Senegal River to the Ebro, ruled from Marrakesh.
fields.t1: Their victory at Sagrajas in 1086 halted Castile's advance and kept much of al-Andalus Muslim for generations.
fields.t2: Overstretched on two fronts, they fell to the Almohads, who used the same charge of impiety the Almoravids once used.
fields.dyk: The Almoravid gold dinar was so trusted that Christian Iberia imitated it as the morabetino, the origin of the Castilian maravedí.
